Rishi — quick technical read and recommendations below. TL;DR: feasible, but hitting p95 <= 350 ms for median/large contexts (9k–30k tokens) will require dedicated resources + caching and tradeoffs on quantization/throughput.

Notes on context window impact
- Cost of attention: attention complexity grows roughly O(n^2) with sequence length for naive attention; optimized kernels and flash attention implementations reduce constant factors, but longer inputs still increase compute and memory.
- KV cache behavior: if most requests share a stable prefix (e.g., common system prompt + repeated history), we can cache key/value tensors for the prefix — that removes re-computing prefix attention for each request and reduces generation latency substantially. If histories are unique per request, cache hit-rate drops and benefit is limited.
- First-token vs tail latency: for very long contexts, the time to process the full context before starting generation increases; streaming can mask some of that by emitting early tokens while later context is processed, but total compute is still needed for coherent long outputs.

Tradeoffs and levers
- Dedicated GPU pool (single-tenant)
  - Pros: consistent latency, ability to pin model variant (pruned/quantized), reserved memory for large contexts.
  - Cons: cost, need capacity planning for bursts.
- Hosted (multi-tenant)
  - Pros: faster time-to-value and autoscaling for unpredictable bursts.
  - Cons: slightly higher tail latency variability and noisy neighbors may push p95 up during peak bursts.
- Caching + prefix reuse
  - Biggest wins when prefix reuse > ~30% across requests. For your workload (if histories repeat across sessions for templates) we should see large p95 improvements.
- Batching
  - Increases throughput and amortizes per-request overhead. But batching introduces latency queuing; to meet tight p95 targets we must cap max batching delay (e.g., micro-batches) and tune batch sizes dynamically.
- Quantization
  - Int8 or lower-bit quantization reduces memory footprint and often improves throughput; may have small quality/regression risks for some model families. Good for Dedicated.
- Streaming
  - Streaming helps perceived latency (first token delivered sooner). However, streaming combined with very large contexts may not reduce total compute; it changes UX more than cost in many cases.

Rough performance heuristics (very approximate)
- Small context (<= 2k tokens) + optimized kernels: single-request p95 can be ~120–250 ms on modern GPU instances when using tuned models and caching.
- Medium context (~9k tokens): p95 moves to ~250–450 ms depending on model and cache effectiveness.
- Very large contexts (20k–32k tokens): p95 commonly exceeds 400–800 ms per request unless we use dedicated, high-memory instances with prefix caching.

Recommendations specific to Nimbus inputs
1) Immediate next step: schedule 60-min scoping with sample prompts and traffic CSV. Marissa + Dev should run a micro-benchmark (2 business days) using a representative sample set.
2) If p95 <= 350 ms is hard requirement for 95th percentile on 9k+ inputs, recommend Dedicated with: 1) pinned model variant, 2) prefix/KV caching enabled, 3) light quantization (int8) and tuned small batch sizes.
3) If you accept slightly higher p95 for very large contexts, we can start on Hosted with caching and Redwood Optimize recommendations and monitor quality/latency — then shift to Dedicated once usage stabilizes.

For benchmarking we need: 5–10 sample prompts across median/95th/peak sizes, a one-day traffic QPS CSV, and your acceptance thresholds (p95/p99 per workload). I can draft a short benchmark plan and cost estimate once we have that.

Happy to join the scoping meeting.
